rv.q: Adrienne Warren gives a powerhouse performance that captures both Turner's explosive energy and her hard-won vulnerability in this crowd-pleasing biomusical.
The show’s flaws fade away next to the star’s incandescence.
Better than Broadway's reigning, mostly enjoyable and definitely money-making example of the genre – the Temptations biomusical Ain't Too Proud
And Adrienne Warren, who nails each impossible note up in that fifth octave and way down in the gravel, every swivel and swagger, and each last defiant, self-actualizing rasp, is simply the best.
The show finds its groove when Ms. Warren is allowed to inhabit the role fully, channeling Turner's fierce energy and distinctive vocal style with impressive conviction.
If you meant to see a true union of song and story, though, you won’t get it here.
Warren delivers a performance of superhuman stamina and skill.

The jukebox biomusical, in which the smoothed-over story of a pop star’s life is turned into the plot of a musical whose score consists of that star’s hit records, is an uncreative bastard genre that has done much damage to Broadway.

The play has been an iconic hallmark of feminist theater but would such a radical work by a new non-white, non-male author make it on the Broadway of today? Katori Hall, one of the few black women playwrights since Hansberry and Shange to see their work on the Great White Way, is the author of Tina’s book (along with Frank Ketelaar and Kees Prins).
This alone is worth the ticket.
Powered by Warren’s hard-charging performance, Tina makes us feel that.
The repetition of the play's mechanics turns all Cyrano’s wit and briskness into an inner torment that goes nowhere.
Warren is electrifying while performing 'Nutbush City Limits' and 'Proud Mary,' continuing to transform herself fully into the legendary performer.
Pretty much every note of nuance is lost in the razzle-dazzle rush.
But like them, Hall’s book covers too much biographical ground too quickly.
The book scenes are straightforward but often overwrought and long-winded, resulting in an inflated running time.
Tina, for all its huffing and puffing, doesn't capture the force of nature she was in live performance.
Warren's performance in the title role has the roaring lift of a helicopter taking flight and the dazzling sparkle of a hundred chandeliers, making Tina a musical not to miss.
It’s just too bad that the show, written by Katori Hall and directed by Phyllida Lloyd (Mamma Mia!), doesn’t live up to her performance.

cn.t: Adrienne Warren's powerhouse performance electrifies this formulaic jukebox bio-musical, with critics praising her transformative embodiment of Turner while finding the by-the-numbers book clunky and uneven.

sg.ra: Per SeatPlan and Headout, center rows D-J are the Lunt-Fontanne sweet spot because the house stage sits unusually high and is not raked — patrons halfway back in orchestra report they cannot see the stage floor, so anchoring forward of the overhang line (row W) but back from rows A-C keeps the stage floor visible.

Front Mezz is only 5 rows deep (A-E) with no balcony above, so every row has clean sightlines — and row B specifically beats row A because a safety railing in front of row A cuts into the stage (one source cites ~35% obstruction for some seats), making B the preferred pick that most guides name by row.

SeatPlan and forum posts flag that the mezzanine overhang starts at row J but begins cutting into the top of the stage from row W back across Left, Center, and Right Orchestra — combined with the Lunt-Fontanne's high unraked stage (floor already hard to see from mid-orchestra), rear orchestra loses both the top and bottom of the picture.

The Lunt-Fontanne has no balcony, so unlike most large Nederlander houses the Rear Mezz has zero overhang — SeatPlan specifically names rows B-C as best because they clear the railing behind the Front Mezz that can obstruct row A, and the section's rake keeps sightlines clean despite being the cheapest seats in the venue.

Multiple guides flag that the Lunt-Fontanne's unusually high, non-raked stage makes rows A-C worse than typical Broadway front rows — Headout and TickPick-linked guides warn sightlines can be obstructed because the stage is raised, and any tall patron in front blocks center-stage action at this proximity.
